title: Mastery Challenge: World Religions
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of World Religions Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
summary: Ten questions, one from each chapter: studying religion, Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Indian, East Asian and newer faiths, religion in the world, and dialogue.

cards.headline: The World Religions Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Questions from across the whole tree, from how scholars define religion to how people of different faiths talk to each other. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: World Religions: mastered
learned: How scholars define, describe and count religions fairly, bracketing the question of truth.
What Jews, Christians and Muslims believe and practice, from covenant and creed to the Five Pillars.
How karma, rebirth and release shape Hindu, Jain, Buddhist and Sikh paths.
How faiths live side by side, from kami and buddhas in Japan to religious freedom in America.
How religion shapes law and protest, and how to weigh doubt, new movements and dialogue fairly.

questions.prompt: You want to describe a faith you've never studied without reducing it to its beliefs. Whose checklist gives you rituals, stories, ethics, community and sacred places too?

options.label: Edward Tylor's
options.rationale: Tylor offered a one-line definition, not a checklist.

options.label: Ninian Smart's seven dimensions
Arnold van Gennep's three stages
options.rationale: Those describe rites of passage only.

options.label: William James's four marks
options.rationale: Those describe mystical states only.

questions.explanation: Smart's seven dimensions cover ritual, experience, narrative, doctrine, ethics, the social side and the material side.

questions.prompt: After Rome destroyed the Second Temple in 70 CE, how did Judaism carry on without its only place of sacrifice?

options.label: Sacrifices moved to a new temple at Yavneh
options.rationale: Yavneh was an academy, not a temple.

options.label: Priests led worship in each Diaspora city
options.rationale: Synagogue worship has no sacrifice, so it needs no priest.

options.label: Jewish practice paused until a third temple
options.rationale: Johanan ben Zakkai ruled that ceremonies could be kept elsewhere.

options.label: Through prayer and study in synagogues, led by rabbis

questions.explanation: Johanan ben Zakkai's academy at Yavneh let Temple ceremonies be kept elsewhere, and the synagogue needs only a minyan of ten, which suited a scattered Diaspora.

questions.prompt: Why did the Council of Nicaea in 325 call the Son homoousios, "of one substance", with the Father?

options.label: To reject Arius's teaching that Christ was a created being
To split the Eastern and Western churches apart
options.rationale: The Nicene Creed is still shared by Catholic, Orthodox and major Protestant churches.

options.label: To add "and the Son" to the line on the Holy Spirit
options.rationale: Western churches added that gradually, from the 6th century.

options.label: To settle which Gospels belong in the New Testament
options.rationale: Nicaea's question was who Christ is.

questions.explanation: Arius taught that Christ was not divine but created; Nicaea's word homoousios declared the Son fully equal with the Father.

questions.prompt: Neither the Quran nor the hadith settles a new question directly. A jurist finds a case the Quran does settle, and extends its reason. What is this method?

options.label: Ijma, the consensus of scholars
options.rationale: Consensus is scholars' agreement, not reasoning from a similar case.

options.label: Isnad, the chain of narrators
options.rationale: The isnad checks how a hadith was passed down.

options.label: Qiyas, reasoning by analogy
Tawhid, asserting God's oneness
options.rationale: Tawhid is a belief about God, not a legal method.

questions.explanation: Qiyas extends a ruling to a new case for the same reason: drugs were ruled forbidden by analogy with the Quran's ban on alcohol, because both intoxicate.

questions.prompt: Why do many Hindus hope for moksha rather than a place in a heavenly realm?

options.label: Hindu texts teach that no heavenly realm exists
options.rationale: Hindus speak of heavenly realms; the point is that a stay there ends.

options.label: Even in a heavenly realm, the self stays only for a time
Moksha means a better rebirth in a wealthy family
options.rationale: Moksha is release from rebirth itself.

options.label: Karma stops working once a person has died
options.rationale: Karma's results may arrive in a future life.

questions.explanation: Karma's results may come even in a heavenly realm, where the self stays only for a time; moksha is release from the whole cycle of rebirth.

questions.prompt: The Four Noble Truths are often compared to a doctor's visit. Which part of the teaching is the diagnosis of what causes the illness?

options.label: Nirvana, the ending of suffering
options.rationale: That's the cure: the third truth says suffering can cease.

options.label: The Eightfold Path, the way to practice
options.rationale: That's the treatment, the fourth truth.

options.label: Dukkha, the uneasiness of a changing world
options.rationale: That's the illness itself, the first truth.

options.label: Craving, a thirst that keeps reaching for more

questions.explanation: The second truth names the cause, craving (tanha). If suffering has a cause, removing the cause can end it.

questions.prompt: A Japanese family takes their newborn to a Shinto shrine, and years later holds a Buddhist funeral for a grandparent. What best explains this?

options.label: Death counts as impure in Shinto, and the faiths are often combined
Japanese law assigns births to shrines and funerals to temples
options.rationale: It's a matter of belief and custom, not law.

options.label: The family must have changed religion between the two events
options.rationale: For many in Japan it's not either-or: the two faiths are combined.

options.label: Shinto shrines are only for festivals, never for family rites
options.rationale: Shrines mark life's beginnings, from newborns to Shichigosan.

questions.explanation: Shrines mark beginnings, but funerals aren't normally held there because death is a source of ritual impurity. Kami and buddhas have been honored together since the late 8th century, like the blending East Asian family of Level 8.

questions.prompt: Which two rules does the First Amendment, ratified in 1791, set for religion in the United States?

options.label: A state church, and freedom to leave it
options.rationale: The amendment forbids an established church.

options.label: Equal funding for every faith, and religious family law
options.rationale: That's closer to India's model.

options.label: No established religion, and free exercise for all
No religious symbols in schools, and no state recognition
options.rationale: That's France's laïcité.

questions.explanation: The Establishment Clause bars an official religion; the Free Exercise Clause protects religious practice.

questions.prompt: How did the Jain ideal of ahimsa come to shape Martin Luther King Jr.'s campaigns?

options.label: King studied under Jain monks in India before 1955
options.rationale: He first met Gandhi's philosophy as a student at Crozer Theological Seminary.

options.label: Through Gandhi, whose satyagraha drew on ahimsa
Baptist churches had taught ahimsa since the Reformation
options.rationale: King's own summary: Christ furnished the spirit, Gandhi the method.

options.label: It didn't; his method came from Christian sources alone
options.rationale: King said Gandhi furnished the method.

questions.explanation: Gandhi, raised in a home with a strong tinge of Jainism, built satyagraha partly on ahimsa; King said Christ furnished the spirit and Gandhi the method.

questions.prompt: The 1893 World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago is regarded as the origin of the modern interfaith movement. What was new about it?

options.label: It merged several faiths into one shared new religion
options.rationale: Dialogue doesn't ask anyone to drop their faith.

options.label: Every faith was given an equal share of the papers
options.rationale: Far from it: English-speaking Christians gave 152 of the 194 papers.

options.label: It ruled on which faiths' teachings were true
options.rationale: Its aim was understanding, not a verdict.

options.label: Faiths met to understand each other, not to defeat each other

questions.explanation: The Parliament brought many faiths to one stage to understand each other. In Swidler's words, the essential purpose of dialogue is to learn.
